name: Polypodium leucotomos

lead: Polypodium leucotomos is a tropical fern extract taken by mouth as an "internal sunscreen" companion, aimed at fewer sunburns, less sun-driven pigmentation and slower photoaging, especially for people who tan.

The extract is rich in antioxidant polyphenols. In studies it reduced UV-induced DNA damage and inflammatory signalling and limited reactive oxygen species. It does not absorb UV the way a sunscreen filter does. Research has examined it for sunburn reactions, melasma, vitiligo and other light-related skin conditions, and a 2025 systematic review of oral photoprotective supplements placed it among the better-supported ones.

paras: People take it as a daily capsule, often before and during sun exposure, and layer it with topical sunscreen. In forums it also appears alongside tanning compounds to reduce how much sun a tan requires. Studied products include Heliocare and Fernblock.

Oral extract is generally well tolerated, with occasional mild stomach upset, headache or itching, and published reviews report no serious adverse effects. Trials are small with varied formulations, so products that do not specify the studied extract may not match them. Studies treat it as an add-on to sunscreen, not a replacement.

web.title: Dermatologic applications of Polypodium leucotomos: a literature review

angle.text: Polypodium leucotomos extract is taken as an internal sunscreen helper: its antioxidants blunt UV skin reactions, aiming at fewer sunburns, less sun-driven dark spots and slower photoaging. Small trials have studied sunburn reactions and pigmentation conditions such as melasma, always alongside topical sunscreen.

lead: Polypodium leucotomos is the older botanical name for Phlebodium aureum, an epiphytic fern native to tropical and subtropical regions of the Americas. Extract from its leaves is sold as an oral supplement, including under the Heliocare name, and has been studied in dermatology as an 'internal' or systemic photoprotective agent [1][2][3].

Decoctions were used in Central American folk medicine, and modern research has examined the extract for conditions including melasma, vitiligo, psoriasis, polymorphous light eruption, atopic dermatitis, postinflammatory hyperpigmentation, photoaging and skin cancer [1]. A 2025 systematic review of oral photoprotective supplements found the greatest evidence among polyphenols, carotenoids and Polypodium leucotomos [4].

Reviews also note limits: few trials support supplements as monotherapy or as an alternative to sunscreen, and trials are small with varied formulations, and several authors of the key trials disclose ties to the company that markets the extract [5][4][6][7]. In looksmaxxing forums it appears as a supplement to combine with tanning peptides and to reduce the sun exposure needed for a tan [3].

The visible payoffs people look for are less sunburn and redness, less UV-driven pigmentation and photoaging, and, for some users, a smoother tan with less direct sun. Dermatologists who describe it generally frame it as a complement to sunscreen and shade, an 'internal' layer rather than a replacement for them.[1][5]

paras: The extract is taken as an adjunct to reduce sunburn, photoaging and pigmentation, sometimes alongside sunscreen [1][4]. A 2009 T Nation poster asked about combining melanotan II with Heliocare and tyrosine to maximise a tan with less time in tanning salons [3].
The extract has been investigated in melasma [8][9][10][11], vitiligo phototherapy [12], actinic keratoses [13] and atopic dermatitis [14]. It has no approved drug indication.

Photoprotection: Wikipedia summarises that clinical studies show oral extract provides photoprotection against UVB and UVA, and that a review of 19 human and 6 basic studies found it well tolerated [1]. A 2019 systematic review and a 2007 nutraceutical review examined its efficacy and safety [15][16]. A 2025 review of 47 studies of oral supplements found the greatest photoprotection evidence for polyphenols, carotenoids and Polypodium leucotomos [4]. A 2021 review concluded that few trials support these supplements as monotherapy, impeding recommendation as an alternative to sunscreen [5].

Recent randomized trials include a 50-volunteer intraindividual study comparing oral nicotinamide with Heliocare Advanced on UVA-induced erythema and thymidine dimers [2], a UVB counterpart [17], and an eight-week trial of a red orange plus Polypodium leucotomos supplement on UVB-induced skin responses [18]. Registered studies examine visible-light effects, minimal erythema dose and skin cancer precursors [19][20][21].

Dermatologic conditions: a randomized placebo-controlled study enrolled 44 patients with generalized vitiligo to test whether oral extract improves NB-UVB repigmentation [12]. A randomized trial examined oral extract, colchicine cream and ingenol mebutate in actinic keratoses [13], and a multicenter trial examined it in atopic dermatitis [14]. Melasma has been studied in registered small trials of 21 and 40 patients [10][11], and a 2025 review covers its dermatologic uses [22].

Study details: a 2017 single-group, self-controlled study in 22 healthy adults with Fitzpatrick skin types I to III gave oral extract before UVB exposure of the back and compared responses with the same participants before supplementation. It reported reduced UVB-induced changes in 17 of 22 subjects on clinical and colorimetry assessment, an 8 percent lower relative erythema intensity, and lower sunburn-cell, thymine-dimer and COX-2 biomarkers on biopsy, with no clear effect on UVA1 or visible-light responses at the doses used. The study was sponsored by the extract's marketer [6].

A 2016 review notes that in a 2-month safety study in 40 people the treated group had fewer sunburns than placebo, that about 30 percent of people with polymorphic light eruption were fully protected from UVA-provoked lesions, and that in a 6-month atopic dermatitis trial in 105 children and adolescents steroid use did not fall significantly while antihistamine use did. It stresses that most human trials were small and some results were borderline [23].

Vitiligo and melasma: a 2014 review summarises randomised trials adding the extract to PUVA or narrowband UVB in generalized vitiligo, with higher repigmentation reported in the extract groups in some studies (for example 40 percent versus 22 percent in one trial of 57 patients, and a significant difference only among high-attendance patients in another), and a 21-woman placebo-controlled melasma trial in which MASI scores fell from 5.7 to 3.3 with the extract while all participants used sunscreen [7]. A 2021 review calls the melasma results mixed, with one study reporting no significant benefit, and notes no monotherapy studies in vitiligo [24]. Several authors of these reviews disclosed consulting roles or grants from the marketer [23][7].

A review of 19 human and 6 basic studies reported that oral extract was well tolerated with a favourable side effect profile [1]. Evidence is based on small trials with different formulations, so supplements that do not specify the studied extract may not be equivalent [4][15].

Phlebodium aureum, known as golden polypody, golden serpent fern or blue-star fern, is a rhizomatous epiphytic fern whose creeping stem is covered in golden-brown scales. Its fronds are 30 to 130 cm long and deeply lobed, and it grows mainly in the canopies of tropical and subtropical forests of the eastern Americas and the Caribbean, from Florida and Georgia south to Paraguay.[1] It is also grown as an ornamental houseplant.[1]

Decoctions of the fern were used in Central American folk medicine as a general tonic prescribed for conditions ranging from asthma to heart disease, and modern research often still uses the older, now-deprecated name Polypodium leucotomos.[1]

A 2021 literature review describes the leaf extract as containing phenolic compounds such as benzoates and cinnamates together with organic acids including quinic, shikimic, glucuronic and malic acid. The most abundant phenolics it lists are p-coumaric, ferulic, caffeic, vanillic and chlorogenic acids, which underlie the extract's antioxidant activity [24]. The review was funded by a company that sells a Polypodium product [24].

A 2021 literature review describes the leaf extract as containing phenolic compounds such as benzoates and cinnamates together with organic acids including quinic, shikimic, glucuronic and malic acid. The most abundant phenolics it lists are p-coumaric, ferulic, caffeic, vanillic and chlorogenic acids, which underlie the extract's antioxidant activity [24]. The review was funded by a company that sells a Polypodium product [24].

The extract is rich in phenolic compounds, and laboratory work attributes antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and immunomodulating properties to it.[16][25] Studies on irradiated skin cells describe reduced formation of reactive oxygen species, lipid peroxidation and erythema, and protection of the cell membrane.[26][27] In fibroblasts exposed to UV, the extract has been reported to influence matrix metalloproteinases, collagen and elastin expression, which are markers linked to photoaging.[27][28] Mouse work reported decreased UV-induced Cox-2 expression and inflammation and enhanced DNA repair.[29] The extract is not a UV filter; its proposed role is to reduce the biological damage after UV reaches the skin.[16][2]

The 2021 review groups proposed actions into antioxidant effects (scavenging reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, inhibiting lipid peroxidation), DNA protection (fewer UV-induced cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and mitochondrial common-deletion damage), anti-inflammatory effects (lower TNF-alpha, COX-2, PGE2 and reduced NF-kB and AP-1 signalling), immunomodulation (limiting the UV-driven conversion of trans- to cis-urocanic acid, which helps preserve Langerhans cells) and extracellular-matrix effects on MMP-1, elastin and fibrillin, mostly from cell and animal work [24]. A 2016 narrative review of animal, cell and human work likewise reports reduced UV-induced inflammatory signalling in human keratinocytes and fibroblasts and reduced sunburn, COX-2 expression and oxidative DNA damage in hairless mice and rats [23].

A 2016 narrative review of animal, cell and human work likewise reports reduced UV-induced inflammatory signalling in human keratinocytes and fibroblasts and reduced sunburn, COX-2 expression and oxidative DNA damage in hairless mice and rats [23].

Earlier human work examined oral extract in healthy volunteers exposed to artificial UV. A study in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology reported that oral extract decreased UV-induced damage to the skin of healthy participants, and a related study reported that orally administered extract decreased psoralen-UVA-induced phototoxicity, pigmentation and damage.[30][31] An earlier paper reported that topical or oral extract prevented acute sunburn and psoralen-induced phototoxic reactions, and reduced depletion of Langerhans cells in human skin.[32] A registered phase II study examined its effect on UVA premutagenic and photoaging markers.[33] Studies describe reduced UV-induced DNA damage markers such as thymidine dimers in volunteers.[2][17]

Community material is sparse. A 2009 T Nation post asks about combining Heliocare with melanotan II and tyrosine to maximise a tan with less time in tanning salons [3]. The logic stated is that the extract might reduce burning and UV damage while a tanning peptide darkens the skin.

More broadly, oral photoprotection is discussed in skincare and anti-ageing circles as an internal layer alongside sunscreen, shade and retinoids, since photoaging, pigmentation and burns are among the visible effects people want to limit [4][5][24].

The extract is sold under several brand names, including Heliocare, and clinical trials in the literature refer to it by names such as Fernblock and Anapsos; the marketer of the Heliocare line is named differently in different sources, and the reviews above disclose consulting and grant ties between several authors and the company that markets the extract [4][6][23][7]. Reviews of supplement photoprotection generally treat the extract as a complement to sunscreen rather than a replacement [5][23][24].
